title: GCSE Chemistry
intro: Exam-style questions on atoms, the periodic table, bonding, moles, rates, organic chemistry and analysis.

questions.prompt: What is the relative charge of an electron?
questions.explanation: Protons have a relative charge of +1, neutrons 0 and electrons −1. Atoms are neutral because they have equal numbers of protons and electrons.

questions.prompt: A sodium atom has a mass number of 23 and an atomic number of 11. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number, so 23 − 11 = 12.

questions.prompt: What is the electronic structure of a chlorine atom (atomic number 17)?
questions.explanation: The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second up to 8, leaving 7 in the outer shell. That is why chlorine is in Group 7.

questions.prompt: Isotopes of an element have different numbers of which particle?
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.

questions.prompt: Which scientist provided evidence for the neutron in 1932?
questions.explanation: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, about 20 years after the nucleus was proposed.

questions.prompt: How does the reactivity of the Group 1 metals change going down the group?
questions.explanation: Going down Group 1, the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases.

questions.prompt: Why are the Group 0 noble gases so unreactive?

options.label: Their outer shell of electrons is full
Their atoms are too heavy to react

questions.explanation: Noble gases have a stable arrangement with a full outer shell, so they do not easily gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.prompt: What is bromine like at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a red-brown liquid at room temperature. Chlorine is a green gas and iodine is a dark grey solid.

questions.prompt: Ionic bonding usually occurs between which types of element?
questions.explanation: Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions and non-metal atoms gain them to form negative ions. The oppositely charged ions attract.

questions.prompt: What is the charge on an oxide ion?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is in Group 6, so an oxygen atom gains two electrons to fill its outer shell, forming O²⁻.

questions.prompt: In graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
questions.explanation: Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others in layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom. That is why graphite conducts electricity.

questions.prompt: Solid ionic compounds conduct electricity.
questions.explanation: In a solid the ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move. Ionic compounds only conduct when melted or dissolved, when the ions are free to move.

questions.prompt: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
What is the value of the Avogadro constant?
questions.explanation: One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles, which is the Avogadro constant.

questions.prompt: In a closed system, the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
questions.explanation: This is the law of conservation of mass. Atoms are not made or destroyed in a reaction, only rearranged.

questions.prompt: 10 g of a solute is dissolved to make 0.5 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
questions.explanation: Concentration = mass ÷ volume, so 10 g ÷ 0.5 dm³ = 20 g/dm³.

questions.prompt: Which ion is present in all acidic solutions?
questions.explanation: Acids release hydrogen ions, H⁺, in water. Alkalis release hydroxide ions, OH⁻.

questions.prompt: During the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, what forms at the negative electrode (cathode)?
questions.explanation: Positive lead ions are attracted to the cathode, where they gain electrons to form lead metal. Bromine forms at the anode.

questions.prompt: A metal carbonate reacts with an acid to make a salt, water and which gas?
questions.explanation: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. The gas turns limewater milky.

questions.prompt: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to energy?

options.label: It is transferred to the surroundings
It is taken in from the surroundings

questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. Combustion is an example.

questions.prompt: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a reaction?

options.label: Particles collide more often and more collisions have enough energy to react

questions.explanation: At higher temperature, particles move faster. They collide more frequently and more collisions have at least the activation energy.

questions.prompt: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?

options.label: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
It gives the particles more energy
It is used up in the reaction

questions.explanation: A catalyst offers a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It is not used up, so it can be reused.

questions.prompt: Cracking large hydrocarbon molecules produces smaller alkanes and alkenes.
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes are used to make polymers.

questions.prompt: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, for example methane, CH₄.

questions.prompt: What happens when bromine water is added to an alkene?

options.label: It turns from orange to colourless
It turns from colourless to orange

questions.explanation: Alkenes have a carbon–carbon double bond that reacts with bromine, decolourising the orange bromine water. Alkanes leave it orange.

questions.prompt: Which process separates crude oil into fractions?
questions.explanation: Crude oil is heated and the vapours condense at different heights in a fractionating column, depending on their boiling points.

questions.prompt: What colour flame does a lithium compound give in a flame test?
questions.explanation: Lithium ions give a crimson flame. Sodium gives yellow, potassium lilac and copper green.

questions.prompt: What is the test for chlorine gas?
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, turning it white. A glowing splint tests for oxygen and a squeaky pop for hydrogen.

questions.prompt: A pure substance melts at a single, specific temperature.
questions.explanation: Pure substances have fixed melting and boiling points. Mixtures melt and boil over a range of temperatures.

questions.prompt: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 3 cm while the solvent moves 6 cm. What is the Rf value?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent, so 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5. Rf values are always less than 1.
